title: 128K+ Long Context Runtime Deep Dive - Titan Analytics
summary: Redwood SEs ran a 60-minute technical deep dive focused on long-context (128k+) runtime behavior: chunking strategies, KV cache persistence, batching/continuous batching, quantization tradeoffs, attention optimizations, and VPC/on-prem deployment constraints. Customer wants a POC to validate 128k+ retrieval-heavy queries with sub-2s tail latency for short answers and acceptable throughput. Action items include providing benchmark artifacts, suggested config profiles, and a pilot plan for Dedicated or Private deployment.
next_steps: Redwood to share 128k benchmark spreadsheet and deck (Ethan)
Customer to provide representative long-doc corpus and target query set (Sana)
Schedule pilot kickoff for Dedicated capacity evaluation (Maya)
action_items: Ethan Cole: share 128k benchmark spreadsheet and kernel-latency plots by 2026-09-22
Sana Rodriguez: deliver 10k sample docs + retrieval queries by 2026-09-25
Maya Patel: send pilot scope + pricing for Dedicated/Private by 2026-09-24
Liam O'Neill: provide VPC network/firewall constraints and KMS requirements by 2026-09-23
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-18 14:00 UTC — Duration 60m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Jared (CTO, Titan), Sana (ML Eng), Liam (Infra), Priya (Security)
---
00:00:05 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through long context, the 128k sessions, and how our runtime behaves under retrieval-heavy loads. hope that's still the right focus?
00:00:18 Jared: Yep, that's perfect. we have customers that shove entire compliance docs + historical chats and expect coherent answers. latency is a big ask—
00:00:26 Sana: —and accuracy, right, we can't hallucinate across chunk boundaries.
00:00:30 Ethan: Totally. today we'll cover chunking strategies, KV/prefix caching, attention memory impacts, batching tradeoffs, and then talk deployment (Dedicated vs Private/VPC) implications. we'll also show profiling data.
00:00:45 Liam: Quick ask — we run in a VPC with strict egress, and want to keep inference on-prem for a pilot. will that change which kernels or quantization paths you can use?
00:00:58 Ravi: good question. kernels are mostly hardware- and build-dependent; on-prem limits us to compiled runtimes we ship for customer HW — we can do most quantized INT8/4 paths but need to validate perf.
00:01:12 Maya: high-level goals: sub-2s tail for short responses, and <500ms per retrieval chunk during indexing for prefetching where possible. is that right Jared?
00:01:23 Jared: Yes. target SLOs are aggressive but worth exploring.
00:01:30 Ethan: ok next slide — our benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat) compares Atlas-8 and Atlas-16 style configs, and shows token-per-second and p99 latency across sequence lengths up to 128k. real note: above ~64k the dominant cost shifts from attention compute to memory bandwidth and KV management.
00:02:00 Sana: wait can you unpack KV management? we rely on persistent KV cache across sessions — is that what you mean?
00:02:08 Ethan: right — two things: 1) per-request KV cache reuse for prefix tokens (so you avoid recomputing prefixes), and 2) large-scale persisted KV store we call cached segments — we stream in chunked KV entries into GPU memory as needed. the runtime supports async prefetch so while token generation is happening we can pull next-chunk KV into memory.
00:02:35 Liam: that prefetching implies network IO from the cache store — how do you guarantee tail latency if cache misses and fetches hit S3 or a remote store?
00:02:47 Ravi: we have a tiered cache model: L0 is in-GPU KV, L1 is host RAM on the instance, L2 is local NVMe, and then object storage. for on-prem you can configure an on-node storage tier so misses don't traverse public network.
00:03:05 Priya: security question — does the KV ever leave the customer's VPC? we need encryption in transit and KMS integration.
00:03:12 Maya: yes, for Private deployments KV and model assets stay in the VPC. we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping; audit logs are available. we'll send the SOC2/ISO docs after.
00:03:28 Jared: good. back to chunking: we plan to chunk at paragraph level, but many docs have important cross-paragraph references. what strategies work best?
00:03:39 Ethan: two common approaches — overlapping window chunking (with overlap ~256-1024 tokens) and semantic chunking (split on embeddings/semantic boundaries). Overlap helps with short-range context coherence; semantic chunking reduces duplication. for 128k, we usually do hybrid: large semantic chunks with small overlap at boundaries for QA tasks.
00:04:05 Sana: and for retrieval, are you storing embeddings for entire 128k documents or per-chunk?
00:04:12 Ethan: per-chunk is typical. you index embeddings per chunk and keep pointers to the original span. retrieval returns top-K chunks which we then stitch or pass as prefixed contexts. stitching at inference time uses KV reuse to avoid recomputation.
00:04:30 Liam: stitching many chunks means many KV loads. how does batching help here?
00:04:36 Ravi: continuous batching is the key — we group small inference requests and reuse KV cache between them. For retrieval-heavy flows we recommend configuring batch windows small (20-50ms) to keep latency tight but still get batching benefits.
00:04:52 Jared: do you have numbers for p50/p95/p99 improvement from batching vs single-token throughput at 128k?
00:05:00 Ethan: in our benchmarks, without batching a single long prefix generate for 128k context can have p99 >> 10s depending on model size. with continuous batching and KV reuse p50 stays similar but p95/p99 improve 2-4x. exact numbers are in the sheet (see the Atlas-16 row).
00:05:20 Sana: quantization — we've seen quality regressions when moving to int4 on generation tasks. what's Redwood's guidance?
00:05:27 Ravi: quantization tradeoffs differ by model family. we recommend mixed strategies: use INT8 for generation-sensitive models and INT4 for embedding-only or reranking. we also provide quantization profiles per model: 'safety-first' (higher precision) vs 'perf-first' (aggressive quant). we'll attach the profiles.
00:05:45 Priya: do quantized BINs still pass your regression eval suite? we need to be sure there are no hallucination spikes on our prompts.
00:05:52 Ethan: we run evals against your prompt set during pilot and flag regressions. for your legal/compliance docs we propose starting with INT8 and moving to INT4 only after a controlled A/B with human evals.
00:06:10 Jared: attention optimizations — can you explain the memory reduction techniques for 128k?
00:06:17 Ethan: yes — two families: algorithmic (sparse/linear attention approximations, locality-sensitive attention) and implementation-level (KV sharding across GPUs, streaming attention where you recompute parts and avoid storing full attention matrices). Redwood supports segmented attention with recompute and fused kernels for better memory efficiency.
00:06:40 Sana: any impact on answer accuracy with segmented or sparse attention?
00:06:45 Ravi: there's a tradeoff. some sparse patterns can degrade cross-chunk reasoning. we typically use hybrid attention — local dense windows plus a global routing layer for important tokens (titles, citations). Model architecture matters; we validate on your workload.
00:07:02 Liam: on the infra side, we'd need to size GPU nodes. what's the recommended inventory for a Dedicated pilot handling 10 rps of retrieval-augmented answers with 128k contexts?
00:07:15 Ethan: rough thumb: for Atlas-8 class (32GB GPUs) you might sustain 1-3 rps depending on sequence length and batching; for Atlas-16/32 (A100-ish) you'd get higher throughput. for 10 rps we recommend a small cluster of 4x Atlas-16-equivalents with autoscale headroom. we'll put specific numbers per model in the spreadsheet.
00:07:40 Jared: that's helpful. does Dedicated give you better KV locality?
00:07:45 Maya: yes, Dedicated means we can co-locate KV and inference on the same instances and tune NVMe tiers; that reduces tail latency significantly vs multi-tenant hosted options.
00:07:56 Priya: on-prem constraints — we have strict egress, and hardware procurement cycles. how long to onboard a Private deployment?
00:08:05 Ravi: typical on-prem installs are 6-8 weeks for first environment (includes package install, network, KMS integration, smoke tests). for cloud VPC private plane it's faster ~2-4 weeks.
00:08:18 Sana: about metrics — what telemetry will we get to debug p99 spikes during heavy retrieval?
00:08:25 Ethan: we expose per-request traces: KV hit/miss, fetch latencies by tier, kernel-level token timings, batch windows, and GC/eviction events. We can stream logs to your Splunk/Datadog.
00:08:40 Liam: what about cold-starts — when you evict KV entries and then a burst of similar queries come, p99 jumps. any mitigations?
00:08:47 Ravi: pre-warming and pinning important prefixes in L0 is effective. also adaptive eviction policies based on query patterns — not pure LRU but frequency+recency. we can configure for your workload.
00:09:05 Jared: could you run a small benchmark on our sample corpus to show p95/p99 improvements with prefetch + pinning?
00:09:12 Maya: yes, that's part of the pilot scope. Ethan will run a focused perf run with your corpus.
00:09:18 Ethan: note on profiling — we instrument kernel timelines and visualize flops vs memory stalls; in many 128k cases the bottleneck is memory copy and NVMe page-ins. we use fused memcpy+kernel scheduling to hide some of that.
00:09:36 Sana: about chunk stitching: when the model needs to reference something across chunk boundaries, how do you surface that without huge context windows?
00:09:44 Ethan: retrieval-first pattern: return top-K semantically relevant chunks and then we build a condensed prompt that summarises or extracts anchors from each chunk (you can also use a condensation model). that keeps generation context small while preserving content. for scenarios that need full fidelity we rely on KV streaming to bring only the tokens relevant to the current attention window.
00:10:05 Liam: hardware question again — do you recommend GPU memory over NVMe heavy nodes for 128k?
00:10:12 Ravi: cost tradeoff: more GPU RAM reduces streaming overhead but increases cost. NVMe-heavy with good prefetching can be economical. For pilot we'd recommend a balanced node with moderate GPU memory and fast NVMe (PCIe4) to validate profile.
00:10:28 Priya: anything special about compliance on Private: audit trails for KV access?
00:10:33 Maya: yes, Private offers detailed audit logs for KV access, KMS envelope operations, and model access events. retention policies are configurable.
00:10:43 Jared: earlier you mentioned attention recompute — does recompute increase latency?
00:10:49 Ethan: recompute trades memory for compute; it can slightly increase latency per token but enables larger effective context. in some workloads the net p99 is better because you avoid expensive NVMe swapping.
00:11:05 Sana: can we do a hybrid where embeddings and retrieval run in one cluster and generation in a higher-memory cluster?
00:11:12 Ravi: absolutely — that's a common architecture. retrieval/embedding nodes are optimized for throughput and can be cheaper; generation nodes are more powerful and can pull in KV as needed.
00:11:24 Liam: networking — if we keep everything in our VPC, what's the expected egress for a pilot vs production?
00:11:30 Maya: depends on number of queries and retrieval sizes. we'll model that in the pilot proposal. we can also co-locate retrieval store to reduce cross-AZ traffic.
00:11:40 Jared: what's the rough cost delta between Dedicated and Private?
00:11:45 Maya: Dedicated is managed infra in Redwood's cloud with reserved capacity pricing; Private is higher fixed platform fee plus infra costs you manage. we'll include price bands in the proposal.
00:11:55 Ethan: ok I'll walk through a short profiling excerpt (link to slides).
00:12:03 Ethan: slide: 128k streaming timeline — you can see phases: retrieval fetch (if miss), KV page-in, token compute, and async prefetch overlap. in our tuned runs prefetch overlaps reduce p50 by ~30% and p95 by ~20%.
00:12:30 Sana: any gotchas with OpenTelemetry traces — does Redwood inject sensitive tokens?
00:12:36 Maya: we can redact payloads; traces include metadata and timings. payload redaction and token redaction are configurable.
00:12:45 Priya: will you sign BAA / extra DPA clauses for on-prem?
00:12:50 Maya: yes, legal will follow up — we'll share standard DPAs and we can accommodate extra clauses for enterprise customers.
00:13:00 Jared: circling back: for our pilot we want reproducible benchmarks showing p95/p99 with and without prefix pinning, and quantization A/B tests. is that feasible?
00:13:10 Ethan: yes — deliverables: benchmark run with your corpus (p50/p95/p99), kernel timeline export, and a model-quality report.
00:13:18 Maya: quick logistics: who owns sample corpus delivery?
00:13:21 Sana: that's us — we'll scrub and share a subset.
00:13:25 Liam: timeline wise we can deliver artifacts by Friday.
00:13:28 Maya: great, we'll schedule pilot kickoff next week.
00:13:35 Ravi: small note on model variants — we suggest testing a 'base' open model + our tuned variant (we provide config/kv/quant profiles) to measure delta.
00:13:48 Jared: are you shipping any custom kernels that require specific driver versions? we control driver versions tightly.
00:13:55 Ethan: yes some fused kernels rely on recent CUDA versions; for Private we'll coordinate driver compatibility matrix. we'll include guidance for driver and OS.
00:14:05 Priya: security follow-up: can we run a STIG-style review?
00:14:10 Maya: yes, we have a questionnaire; we'll send it.
00:14:15 Jared: ok any more deep technical items?
00:14:20 Sana: one: how do you handle deterministic tokenization across chunk boundaries if we do modified tokenizers?
00:14:26 Ethan: tokenization determinism is critical — we support shipping tokenizer binaries and ensure consistent token offsets; we log tokenization maps for debugging.
00:14:36 Maya: I'll pause and open to questions —
00:14:40 Speaker 1 (Jared): can you just also add a note about model rollbacks if quality regresses mid-pilot?
00:14:46 Maya: yes we support rollback to pinned model artifacts and automatic traffic split; we'll show rollback runbooks.
00:14:55 Ethan: quick demo idea — we can run a 10-minute perf run during pilot kickoff to surface real p99 numbers.
00:15:02 Jared: fine by us.
00:15:10 Maya: ok I'll recap next steps at the end. moving on to a few detailed questions from Liam on kernel scheduling.
00:15:20 Liam: when you have multiple concurrent requests with different sequence lengths, how do you avoid head-of-line blocking in the GPU queue?
00:15:29 Ravi: we partition into priority lanes: latency-critical small requests and throughput-y long requests. the scheduler will interleave kernels and prioritize small requests to avoid them being blocked behind a long 128k job.
00:15:45 Sana: do you splice long jobs into smaller micro-batches to help interleave?
00:15:50 Ethan: yes we break long generation into segments that yield periodically, letting the scheduler place short requests in between.
00:15:58 Jared: what about memory fragmentation over long runs?
00:16:02 Ravi: we have periodic compaction and slab allocators to reduce fragmentation; in Private we can tune GC frequency.
00:16:12 Maya: short break — we'll pick back up on pilot scoping and timelines.
00:16:20 [~5 minute silence/background chatter as folks switch docs]
00:21:25 Ethan: ok back — pilot scope proposal: 2-week perf validation, 4-week functional validation (quality/regression), then a 6-week production pilot if both pass.
00:21:40 Jared: acceptance criteria for perf validation?
00:21:44 Maya: p95 within 2x of baseline target and p99 under the SLO range we discussed; quality regression <1% on your eval metrics.
00:21:55 Sana: baseline target = sub-2s tail for short answers?
00:22:00 Maya: correct for short answers. for long generated reports we'll define separate SLOs.
00:22:08 Liam: cost caps for pilot?
00:22:12 Maya: we'll include a soft cap in the proposal and alerting on projected spend.
00:22:20 Priya: please include data residency language.
00:22:23 Maya: will do.
00:22:30 Ethan: quick note — open-source models vary a lot; if you want guaranteed fidelity we also offer Redwood-verified model profiles that we can prioritize.
00:22:40 Jared: ok let's wrap.
00:22:44 Maya: recap of next steps: Ethan to share benchmarks + slides; Sana to share corpus; Maya to send pilot scope/pricing; Liam to give VPC/KMS constraints.
00:22:58 Sana: we'll also include the top-50 retrieval queries that drive p99 historically.
00:23:05 Maya: perfect. any final questions?
00:23:10 Jared: no, thanks everyone. good session.
00:23:15 Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with notes and the security deck.
00:23:20 [meeting ends — actual call lasted about 60 minutes; remainder was follow-up chat]
---
Notes about transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few misattributed turns and occasional word swaps (e.g., Atlas vs Atlas-16 typed as 'Atlas 16' etc.). Recordings, slides, and the benchmark spreadsheet were shared in the meeting chat (links).
